Let’s dive into Chapter 8: The Ethics of Wealth—Earning, Spending, and the Spirit of Generosity.
Money is woven into nearly every part of our lives. It opens doors, sure, but it can also bring its own set of challenges.
The Sunan Ibn Majah doesn’t shy away from this reality. Instead, it gives us down-to-earth advice on how to earn, spend, and share what we have in ways that honor both ourselves and those around us.
Picture this: a shopkeeper at the end of a long day, counting his earnings. He feels proud—he’s worked hard. But then, he remembers the Prophet’s words: wealth isn’t just something to celebrate—it’s a trust. Not just a personal victory.
The hadith talk a lot about how we earn our living. They encourage honesty, warn against deceit, and remind us to treat employees and customers fairly. There’s a story about a merchant who was tempted to cut corners—maybe fudge the numbers for a bigger profit. But he chose to stick with his integrity, even if it meant earning a little less. What happened? His reputation grew, and soon, loyal customers flocked to his shop. That’s real success.
When it comes to spending, the teachings are clear: don’t go overboard. The Prophet warns against extravagance and waste. He urges us to live within our means and, if possible, avoid debt.
I want you to imagine a family that enjoyed a season of plenty—maybe a few good harvests or a big bonus at work. Then, suddenly, times got tough. They remembered a simple teaching: the best wealth is the kind that’s enough. So, they pared down, focused on what really mattered, and found something priceless—contentment and peace.
Generosity is another big theme. The Prophet actually encouraged folks to give freely, to support those who needed it, and not expect anything in return. Think of a young woman with only a small meal to her name, yet she shares it with a hungry stranger. That one act of kindness? It sparked a wave of generosity across her whole community.
Of course, it’s not always easy. The hadith warn us to look out for greed and envy. There’s a story about two friends—one wealthy, one struggling. Jealousy crept in, and it put a strain on their bond. But when they asked for advice, they were reminded: real wealth isn’t about what you own. It’s about gratitude and contentment.
Most of us don’t even realize how quickly money can stir up anxiety or drive a wedge between people. But the teachings in Sunan Ibn Majah offer a different way to see things. Wealth is just a tool—not the finish line. It’s meant to be used wisely, shared with a generous heart, and never allowed to overshadow the values of honesty, compassion, and community.
